screens.title: Introduction to Ethernet and LAN Switching
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will ground your understanding of Ethernet and how Layer 2 switching makes local networks efficient. Ethernet is the set of standards that define both the physical connections and the frame format used to carry higher‑level data. Frames include source and destination MAC addresses, a type/length field, and an error check that helps devices detect transmission errors. MAC addresses are the hardware identifiers burned into network interfaces, and switches use them to make forwarding decisions. You will learn how a switch dynamically builds a MAC address table by observing source addresses, then forwards, filters, or floods frames according to what it knows. We will also explain the difference between collision domains and broadcast domains — why switches eliminate collisions per port but still flood broadcasts across a single Layer 2 domain. Finally, you will see the basic Cisco IOS commands that let you inspect a switch’s MAC address table and interface state. By the end you’ll understand the core behaviors that let modern LANs scale and operate reliably.

Introduction to Ethernet and LAN Switching

Understand the frame, the address, and the switch behaviors that make LANs efficient and scalable.

In this lesson

Ethernet frame structure, MAC addressing, switch learning and forwarding, domain differences, and basic Cisco commands.

Why it matters

Knowing Layer 2 behavior helps you troubleshoot connectivity and design networks that avoid unnecessary flooding and collisions.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain Ethernet frame structure, identify and interpret MAC addresses, and describe the core behaviors of a Layer 2 switch. You will practice reading a switch’s MAC address table and use basic Cisco IOS commands to confirm which devices are connected to specific ports. Understanding these skills matters because they let you diagnose local connectivity, verify where traffic flows, and distinguish problems caused by physical cabling from issues at Layer 2. For example, when you see a device’s MAC mapped to an unexpected port, you can track whether a network move or mispatch occurred. You will also learn to differentiate collision domains from broadcast domains, which prevents incorrect troubleshooting assumptions that colliding traffic is caused by higher layer issues. This set of objectives gives you the foundation to manage and troubleshoot small to medium LANs confidently.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on practice: using a Cisco switch to confirm MAC learning and checking interface status. You will learn the sequence of steps to connect to a switch, enter privileged EXEC mode, run the show mac address-table command, and interpret entries such as dynamic or static records and the VLAN and port assignment. You will also practice verifying a specific interface with the show interfaces command to confirm operational state, speed, and duplex. These skills matter because many Layer 2 problems are caused by mispatches or mismatched interface settings, not higher layer protocols. For example, if a device doesn’t appear in the MAC table after a ping, you’ll check physical link, then interface details. By practicing these commands you build a habit of methodical troubleshooting that reduces diagnostic time and prevents misdiagnosis.

screens.title: Ethernet frame structure
screens.narratorSegment: An Ethernet frame is the packet format used at Layer 2 to carry higher layer data across a local network. The frame begins with a preamble and start delimiter that synchronize receivers, then includes the destination MAC and source MAC addresses. After those addresses you find the type or length field which tells the receiver how to interpret the payload, followed by the payload itself and a Frame Check Sequence for error detection. A concrete example: a workstation sending a file will encapsulate the IP packet inside the Ethernet payload, and the NIC will set the source MAC to the workstation’s hardware address and the destination MAC to the next hop’s address. One common misconception is treating MACs like IP addresses — MACs identify interfaces on the same link and are not routable across IP networks. Another misunderstanding is expecting the FCS to correct errors; it only detects them so devices drop corrupted frames. Key takeaway: the destination and source MAC fields are what switches read to learn and forward traffic, and understanding each frame field helps you interpret captures and CLI outputs accurately. Consider: how would a switch behave if the source MAC field were blank or incorrect?

keyIdea.title: Frame fields
keyIdea.text: Destination and source MACs plus type/length and FCS define how frames are delivered and verified on a LAN.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Ethernet frame structure
Frame breakdown
Destination MAC
Identifies the intended receiver at Layer 2; switches use it to forward frames to the right port.
Source MAC
The sender’s hardware address; switches learn this and record it in the MAC table.
Type/Length & Payload
Indicates the protocol in the payload or the size of the payload data.
Frame Check Sequence
A CRC used to detect transmission errors; frames with a bad FCS are discarded.
Concrete example
A host sends an IP packet to a printer on the same LAN. The host sets its NIC’s source MAC and the printer's MAC as destination. The switch uses the destination MAC to forward the frame only to the printer’s port if known.
Common misconception
MAC addresses are not routable like IP addresses; they apply only within the local link. Routers operate on IP addresses to forward across networks.
Key Takeaway

Ethernet frames carry the MAC addresses that switches use to learn and forward traffic; FCS detects corruption but does not correct it.

screens.title: MAC addresses explained
screens.narratorSegment: A MAC address is a 48‑bit identifier assigned to a network interface controller. It is usually shown as six octets in hexadecimal, for example 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E. The first half of the address often indicates the vendor, while the second half is a unique identifier for the interface. Switches depend on these identifiers to distinguish devices on the same LAN segment. A practical example is when a laptop moves and gets a new IP via DHCP but retains the same MAC; the switch will still learn the device at the new port by observing the source MAC in frames. A common error is assuming MACs change whenever IPs change; they do not unless the NIC is replaced or a virtual MAC is used. Another misconception is that MAC addresses are perfectly guaranteed unique in all deployments; while globally administered MACs are intended to be unique, virtual adapters or misconfigured equipment can cause duplicates and lead to unexpected learning behavior. Remember: MACs are the stable Layer 2 identity switches use to map ports to devices. MAC addresses explained means macs are stable layer 2 identifiers used by switches to map devices to physical ports, typically shown as six hex octets.. In practical terms, what 48 bits mean and how addresses appear in practice. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › MAC addresses explained
MAC structure
48 bits displayed as six groups of two hex digits. Example format: 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E. The Organizationally Unique Identifier in the first three octets often identifies the vendor.
Vendor/OUI
First three octets indicate manufacturer assignment.
Interface ID
Last three octets provide a unique identifier for the NIC.
Example scenario
A laptop with MAC 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E moves from GigabitEthernet0/1 to GigabitEthernet0/5. The switch learns the MAC on the new port when the laptop sends traffic, updating the MAC table dynamically.
Misconception
MAC addresses do not change when IP addresses change. Treat MACs as Layer 2 identifiers and IPs as Layer 3 addresses for routing decisions.
Practical check
If two devices show the same MAC in a MAC table, investigate virtual adapters, spoofing, or misconfigured equipment before assuming a switch problem.
Key Takeaway

A MAC is a hardware identity used by switches to map devices to ports; understanding its format helps you interpret table entries and spot duplicates.

screens.title: How a switch learns MAC addresses
screens.narratorSegment: Switch learning is a simple, passive process that occurs whenever a switch receives a frame. When a frame arrives, the switch inspects the source MAC and records a mapping of that MAC to the ingress port in its MAC address table, often called the CAM table. This entry is usually marked dynamic and may age out after a period of inactivity. For example, when Host A sends to Host B, the switch learns Host A’s MAC from the incoming frames on port Gi0/1. A common misconception is thinking the switch actively queries devices to discover addresses; it does not. Learning is triggered only by observed traffic. Another important point: if a device moves ports or is replaced, the switch updates the table automatically when the next frame with that source MAC is seen. Concrete example: after moving a laptop to a new port, pinging another host will produce frames that let the switch relearn the MAC at the new port. Takeaway: monitoring the MAC table after traffic generation is how you confirm where devices are connected. How a switch learns MAC addresses means switches learn passively from source macs in observed frames and update the mac table dynamically without active discovery.. In practical terms, the dynamic process that builds the mac (cam) table. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › How a switch learns MAC addresses
Step-by-step learning
1. Frame arrives
Switch inspects the Ethernet frame's source MAC and the port it arrived on.
2. Update CAM table
Switch records MAC-to-port mapping as a dynamic entry, with an aging timer.
3. Aging and refresh
If no traffic from that MAC appears before the timer expires, the entry is removed.
Concrete example
Laptop A on Gi0/1 sends a ping. The switch records Laptop A's MAC with port Gi0/1. Later, Laptop A moves to Gi0/5 and sends traffic; the switch updates the mapping to Gi0/5 when it sees traffic from that MAC on the new port.
Misconception
Switches do not poll hosts to learn MACs. Learning only happens when a host transmits frames that include its source MAC.
Key Takeaway

Switches learn passively from source MACs and update their MAC table dynamically; generate traffic to force learning after moves.

screens.title: Forwarding, Filtering, and Flooding
screens.narratorSegment: A switch takes one of three actions when it receives a frame: forwarding, filtering, or flooding. Forwarding happens when the switch finds the destination MAC in its MAC table mapped to a port different from the ingress port; it then forwards the frame only to that destination port, which conserves bandwidth and isolates traffic. Filtering occurs when the destination MAC is associated with the same port the frame arrived on — the switch understands the source and destination are on the same segment and drops the frame to avoid unnecessary traffic. Flooding occurs when the destination is unknown or is the broadcast address; the switch sends the frame to all ports except the ingress port so the intended recipient will receive it and respond, allowing the switch to learn its location. A concrete example: if Host A sends to Host B and the switch knows Host B on Gi0/2, the frame is forwarded to Gi0/2. A common misconception is assuming a switch behaves like a router for unknown addresses — it does not route; it floods for unknown Layer 2 destinations. Closing question: when would flooding at Layer 2 cause operational issues in a large network?

keyIdea.title: Decision rules
keyIdea.text: Switch behavior depends on MAC table knowledge: forward when known, filter when same port, flood when unknown or broadcast.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Forwarding, Filtering, and Flooding
Switch decision logic
Forwarding
Destination MAC found and mapped to a different port → send only to that port.
Filtering
Destination mapped to the same port the frame arrived on → drop it to avoid reflection.
Flooding
Destination unknown or broadcast → send out all other ports so the frame reaches every device in the broadcast domain.
Concrete example
Frame arrives on Gi0/5 with destination MAC mapped to Gi0/2: switch forwards this frame only to Gi0/2. If mapping is absent, the switch floods all ports except Gi0/5.
Troubleshooting pitfall
Seeing many unknown unicast floods may indicate aging timers, duplicated MACs, or devices not sending traffic; generate traffic to populate the table and investigate duplicates.
Key Takeaway

Switches forward when they know the destination, filter same‑port traffic, and flood when unknown or broadcast; controlling floods is key to performance.

screens.title: Collision domains vs Broadcast domains
screens.narratorSegment: Collision domains and broadcast domains are two different ways to think about how traffic flows on a LAN. A collision domain is a segment where frames can collide if two devices transmit at the same time. In older hub-based networks, the entire collision domain could be the whole hub; modern switches create separate collision domains per port, so two ports can transmit simultaneously without collisions. A broadcast domain is a set of nodes that receive broadcast frames from each other at Layer 2. By default, all ports on a single Layer 2 switch belong to the same broadcast domain, so a broadcast from one host is flooded to all other ports. A common confusion is assuming switches isolate broadcasts the same way they isolate collisions; they do not by default. The only way to segment broadcast domains on the same switch is to use VLANs or route the traffic through a router, which operates at Layer 3. Concrete example: sending an ARP request is a broadcast that every host on the switch will receive unless VLANs separate them. Takeaway: switches reduce collisions but not broadcasts by default — plan VLANs when broadcast containment is required.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Collision vs Broadcast domains
Collision domain
A region where frames can collide when sent simultaneously. Switch ports typically create separate collision domains, so collisions are limited to a single link.
Why it matters
Reducing collision domains improves throughput and reduces retransmissions on a LAN.
Broadcast domain
A logical set of devices that receive broadcast frames from each other. By default, all ports on a switch share a broadcast domain and receive broadcasts such as ARP requests.
Containment
To limit broadcasts, use VLANs or route between networks. Routers segment broadcast domains because they do not forward Layer 2 broadcasts.
Example
ARP broadcast from Host A reaches all other hosts on the same switch unless VLANs are configured.
Misconception
Switches do not automatically segment broadcast domains by port; VLANs are required.
Key Takeaway
Switches isolate collision domains per port but leave the broadcast domain intact by default; use VLANs to contain broadcasts.

screens.title: Using Cisco IOS to inspect the MAC table
screens.narratorSegment: Using IOS commands is how you confirm what a switch has learned. The primary command is show mac address-table, which lists learned MAC addresses, their VLAN, type, and the associated port. A typical line might show Vlan 1, then a MAC written as 001a.2b3c.4d5e, marked DYNAMIC, and Gi0/1 as the port. Start by entering privileged EXEC mode with enable, then run show mac address-table. If you want details about a specific interface, use show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/1 to verify link state, speed, and duplex. A concrete walkthrough: enable, show mac address-table, locate the MAC of interest, then run show interfaces on the listed port to check whether the interface is up. One misconception is relying solely on the MAC table to prove reachability; a MAC entry shows the switch saw traffic from that MAC, but it doesn't prove the device currently responds. Always pair MAC table inspection with interface status and generated traffic like a ping. Final question: after moving a host, why might you have to generate traffic before the MAC table reflects the new port? Using Cisco IOS to inspect the MAC table means use show mac address-table and show interfaces to confirm where a device is learned and whether its port is operational.. In practical terms, commands and how to interpret their output. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Inspect the MAC table
Terminal walkthrough
enable
show mac address-table
-- sample output --
Vlan    Mac Address       Type      Ports
1       001a.2b3c.4d5e    DYNAMIC   Gi0/1
Read the VLAN, MAC, type (DYNAMIC/STATIC), and port. Use this to map a device physical location in the switch wiring.
Check interface

-- shows status, speed, duplex, and error counters --
Concrete example
After moving a host, ping another device. Then run show mac address-table; the switch updates the entry when it observes the host's source MAC on the new port.
Key Takeaway

Combine MAC table inspection with interface status and generated traffic to verify connectivity and device location accurately.

screens.title: Hands-on activity: explore MAC table and port status
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity guides you through a simple lab verification using a Cisco switch. Begin by connecting to the switch console or SSH and enter privileged EXEC mode with the enable command. Run show mac address-table to list learned addresses. Identify a MAC you care about and note the associated port and VLAN. Next, run show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/1 (or the listed port) to confirm the interface is up, its speed and duplex, and whether there are error counters. A practical tip: if you do not see the MAC you expect, generate traffic from the endpoint—such as a ping—to ensure the switch receives frames to learn from. A common error is assuming an absence of an entry proves the device is disconnected; sometimes the device simply has not sent traffic since the switch booted or its entry aged out. After performing these steps, reflect on how the MAC table and interface status together provide a more complete picture of link health and device reachability. The VLAN column indicates which Layer 2 broadcast domain the entry belongs to and is useful in environments where multiple VLANs exist. screens.title: Common troubleshooting errors
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting at Layer 2 often fails when practitioners make a few predictable mistakes. First, assuming a missing MAC table entry means the device is offline. In reality, the device may simply not have sent traffic recently; trigger a ping to force learning. Second, confusing switch and router roles: switches forward based on MACs within a broadcast domain, while routers move packets between networks using IP addresses and break broadcast domains. Third, ignoring physical layer problems: bad cables, incorrect speed or duplex settings, and port errors often cause perceived Layer 2 failures. A concrete example: a NIC configured for half duplex connected to a switch set to full duplex can cause collisions and poor throughput — check show interfaces for mismatches. Finally, misinterpreting flooding: unknown unicast flooding is the switch’s normal behavior for unknown destinations, not necessarily a malfunction. Takeaway: pair MAC table checks with interface diagnostics and generated traffic to avoid false conclusions. screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Keep three core ideas in mind as you work with Ethernet and switches. First, Ethernet frames carry source and destination MAC addresses and an FCS for error detection; these fields are what switches inspect to forward traffic. Second, switches learn passively — they populate a MAC address table from observed source MACs and use that table to forward, filter, or flood frames; dynamic entries age out while static entries persist. Third, switches segment collision domains per port but do not segment broadcast domains by default; broadcasts are flooded to all ports in the same Layer 2 domain unless VLANs are used. A quick reflective question: when you inspect a MAC table and see unexpected mappings, what three checks will you perform first? The answer: verify interface status, generate traffic from the endpoint, and inspect physical cabling or VLAN membership.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will ground your understanding of Ethernet and how Layer 2 switching makes local networks efficient. Ethernet is the set of standards that define both the physical connections and the frame format used to carry higher‑level data. Frames include source and destination MAC addresses, a type/length field, and an error check that helps devices detect transmission errors. MAC addresses are the hardware identifiers burned into network interfaces, and switches use them to make forwarding decisions. You will learn how a switch dynamically builds a MAC address table by observing source addresses, then forwards, filters, or floods frames according to what it knows. We will also explain the difference between collision domains and broadcast domains — why switches eliminate collisions per port but still flood broadcasts across a single Layer 2 domain. Finally, you will see the basic Cisco IOS commands that let you inspect a switch’s MAC address table and interface state. By the end you’ll understand the core behaviors that let modern LANs scale and operate reliably.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain Ethernet frame structure, identify and interpret MAC addresses, and describe the core behaviors of a Layer 2 switch. You will practice reading a switch’s MAC address table and use basic Cisco IOS commands to confirm which devices are connected to specific ports. Understanding these skills matters because they let you diagnose local connectivity, verify where traffic flows, and distinguish problems caused by physical cabling from issues at Layer 2. For example, when you see a device’s MAC mapped to an unexpected port, you can track whether a network move or mispatch occurred. You will also learn to differentiate collision domains from broadcast domains, which prevents incorrect troubleshooting assumptions that colliding traffic is caused by higher layer issues. This set of objectives gives you the foundation to manage and troubleshoot small to medium LANs confidently.

This second objectives slide focuses on practice: using a Cisco switch to confirm MAC learning and checking interface status. You will learn the sequence of steps to connect to a switch, enter privileged EXEC mode, run the show mac address-table command, and interpret entries such as dynamic or static records and the VLAN and port assignment. You will also practice verifying a specific interface with the show interfaces command to confirm operational state, speed, and duplex. These skills matter because many Layer 2 problems are caused by mispatches or mismatched interface settings, not higher layer protocols. For example, if a device doesn’t appear in the MAC table after a ping, you’ll check physical link, then interface details. By practicing these commands you build a habit of methodical troubleshooting that reduces diagnostic time and prevents misdiagnosis.

An Ethernet frame is the packet format used at Layer 2 to carry higher layer data across a local network. The frame begins with a preamble and start delimiter that synchronize receivers, then includes the destination MAC and source MAC addresses. After those addresses you find the type or length field which tells the receiver how to interpret the payload, followed by the payload itself and a Frame Check Sequence for error detection. A concrete example: a workstation sending a file will encapsulate the IP packet inside the Ethernet payload, and the NIC will set the source MAC to the workstation’s hardware address and the destination MAC to the next hop’s address. One common misconception is treating MACs like IP addresses — MACs identify interfaces on the same link and are not routable across IP networks. Another misunderstanding is expecting the FCS to correct errors; it only detects them so devices drop corrupted frames. Key takeaway: the destination and source MAC fields are what switches read to learn and forward traffic, and understanding each frame field helps you interpret captures and CLI outputs accurately. Consider: how would a switch behave if the source MAC field were blank or incorrect?

A MAC address is a 48‑bit identifier assigned to a network interface controller. It is usually shown as six octets in hexadecimal, for example 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E. The first half of the address often indicates the vendor, while the second half is a unique identifier for the interface. Switches depend on these identifiers to distinguish devices on the same LAN segment. A practical example is when a laptop moves and gets a new IP via DHCP but retains the same MAC; the switch will still learn the device at the new port by observing the source MAC in frames. A common error is assuming MACs change whenever IPs change; they do not unless the NIC is replaced or a virtual MAC is used. Another misconception is that MAC addresses are perfectly guaranteed unique in all deployments; while globally administered MACs are intended to be unique, virtual adapters or misconfigured equipment can cause duplicates and lead to unexpected learning behavior. Remember: MACs are the stable Layer 2 identity switches use to map ports to devices. Switch learning is a simple, passive process that occurs whenever a switch receives a frame. When a frame arrives, the switch inspects the source MAC and records a mapping of that MAC to the ingress port in its MAC address table, often called the CAM table. This entry is usually marked dynamic and may age out after a period of inactivity. For example, when Host A sends to Host B, the switch learns Host A’s MAC from the incoming frames on port Gi0/1. A common misconception is thinking the switch actively queries devices to discover addresses; it does not. Learning is triggered only by observed traffic. Another important point: if a device moves ports or is replaced, the switch updates the table automatically when the next frame with that source MAC is seen. Concrete example: after moving a laptop to a new port, pinging another host will produce frames that let the switch relearn the MAC at the new port. Takeaway: monitoring the MAC table after traffic generation is how you confirm where devices are connected. A switch takes one of three actions when it receives a frame: forwarding, filtering, or flooding. Forwarding happens when the switch finds the destination MAC in its MAC table mapped to a port different from the ingress port; it then forwards the frame only to that destination port, which conserves bandwidth and isolates traffic. Filtering occurs when the destination MAC is associated with the same port the frame arrived on — the switch understands the source and destination are on the same segment and drops the frame to avoid unnecessary traffic. Flooding occurs when the destination is unknown or is the broadcast address; the switch sends the frame to all ports except the ingress port so the intended recipient will receive it and respond, allowing the switch to learn its location. A concrete example: if Host A sends to Host B and the switch knows Host B on Gi0/2, the frame is forwarded to Gi0/2. A common misconception is assuming a switch behaves like a router for unknown addresses — it does not route; it floods for unknown Layer 2 destinations. Closing question: when would flooding at Layer 2 cause operational issues in a large network?

Collision domains and broadcast domains are two different ways to think about how traffic flows on a LAN. A collision domain is a segment where frames can collide if two devices transmit at the same time. In older hub-based networks, the entire collision domain could be the whole hub; modern switches create separate collision domains per port, so two ports can transmit simultaneously without collisions. A broadcast domain is a set of nodes that receive broadcast frames from each other at Layer 2. By default, all ports on a single Layer 2 switch belong to the same broadcast domain, so a broadcast from one host is flooded to all other ports. A common confusion is assuming switches isolate broadcasts the same way they isolate collisions; they do not by default. The only way to segment broadcast domains on the same switch is to use VLANs or route the traffic through a router, which operates at Layer 3. Concrete example: sending an ARP request is a broadcast that every host on the switch will receive unless VLANs separate them. Takeaway: switches reduce collisions but not broadcasts by default — plan VLANs when broadcast containment is required.

Keep three core ideas in mind as you work with Ethernet and switches. First, Ethernet frames carry source and destination MAC addresses and an FCS for error detection; these fields are what switches inspect to forward traffic. Second, switches learn passively — they populate a MAC address table from observed source MACs and use that table to forward, filter, or flood frames; dynamic entries age out while static entries persist. Third, switches segment collision domains per port but do not segment broadcast domains by default; broadcasts are flooded to all ports in the same Layer 2 domain unless VLANs are used. A quick reflective question: when you inspect a MAC table and see unexpected mappings, what three checks will you perform first? The answer: verify interface status, generate traffic from the endpoint, and inspect physical cabling or VLAN membership.

As a quick reference, remember these three compact rules. Rule one: switches read source and destination MACs in Ethernet frames to populate the MAC table and make forwarding decisions. Rule two: forwarding sends frames to a single port when the destination is known; unknown unicast and broadcast frames are flooded to all ports except the ingress port. Rule three: a switch separates collision domains per port but keeps broadcast domains intact by default; use VLANs or routing to partition broadcasts. These short reminders capture the operational facts you'll apply when inspecting switch behavior and running show commands. Final reflection: when you see unexpected behavior, which of these three rules helps you form your first diagnostic hypothesis?
